utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Chester Stamp, Ekkehard Withopf, and our -- today's case manager, Mr. Hasan Younis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids good morning to everyone present and greets specifically the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, and all the personnel in this courtroom. We have a planned witness for today. But before beginning his testimony, the Chamber wishes first to render a decision regarding the question of documents and, also, to address the question of the duration of the cross-examination. Regarding the latter, the Chamber requests that when there is a cross-examination, that for both Defence teams the cross-examination should not exceed the time accorded and used by the Prosecution plus 50 per cent. By way of example, if the Prosecution took one hour, the Defence counsel together would have one and a half hours. This is a rule of principle, of thumb. But should the need arise to extend that time limit, the Defence will tell us that for this or that reason they need some additional time beyond this rule. All this is designed in order to economise our energy and to avoid any unnecessary waste of time. The decision that we are rendering - and I have provided a copy to the interpreters and I'm going to read the decision, and I ask the parties to take note of it. In order to enable the proceedings to evolve in the best possible conditions and in order to economise with the time, and bearing in mind the interests of justice, the Chamber has asked the Defence to convey its position regarding the admission into evidence of documents consisting of several hundred examples. The Chamber had earlier asked the Prosecution to provide a consolidated list of documents. It was thus that Annexes A and B were provided. The Chamber was informed in writing by -- of the fact that more than 600 documents are challenged. The Chamber was also informed by the Defence that some of the documents are contested on the basis of relevance, some on the basis of their authenticity, and others on the basis of the chain of custody. The Chamber has taken note of the position of the Prosecution, which wishes to have these documents tendered into evidence as part of its case. The Chamber wishes to underline that introducing documents solely through witnesses would result in a considerable extension of the time needed for hearing witnesses and would have adverse effects on the efficiency of the process, of the proceedings. In order to resolve any potential -- avoid any potential difficulties, the Chamber will discuss the admissibility of documents after having asked the Defence to reason their challenges. For that purpose, the Chamber requests that the Prosecution provide it as soon as possible with a copy of the documents so that they may be given a number, that is, that they be marked for identification. The Chamber also requests that the Defence elaborate in writing the grounds for contesting the documents, document by document, following the order of those documents in Annex A and Annex B, and indicating its arguments regarding relevance, authenticity, the chain of custody of the said documents, or any other grounds. Consequently, the Defence will communicate its submissions in writing before Thursday, 8th of April, 2004 at 1600 hours. The Prosecution for its part will have until Monday, the 19th of April, 1600 hours, to respond. Should the Defence have any problems regarding this timetable, it will be allowed - that is, the Defence - to have an additional week, which would mean the date will be delayed until Thursday, the 15th of April, and then of course under those conditions the Prosecution will also get an additional week. But it is up to the Defence to indicate any difficulties if it is unable to respect the deadline of the 8th of April that has been decided by the Chamber. Finally, should the destiny of certain documents not be resolved by written submissions, the Chamber will subsequently hold a special hearing to address those particular documents. Therefore, the Chamber would kindly ask you to read through this decision carefully. Therefore, to summarise: The Prosecution needs to provide us with one copy of each document, not three, to save time. And the Chamber wishes to thank in advance the Prosecution for all the efforts it will have to make. The Chamber is fully aware of all the efforts being invested by all the parties in order to facilitate all our tasks. And also, the Defence is being asked, as indicated in the decision, to tell us document by document why they are challenging the admissibility of those documents. And then on the basis of the written submissions of the Defence and those of the Prosecution, we will rule regarding the 655 documents. And if we are unable to make a decision regarding certain documents on the basis of those submissions of the Defence and the Prosecution, we will have a separate hearing to deal with those documents. So without any further ado, I should like to ask the witness to be brought into the courtroom. Would Madam Usher be kind enough to go and fetch the witness. Should the Defence during the break find that the deadline of the 8th of April is too soon, let us know and we will grant you an additional week. But it is up to you. As there's going to be a break of several days, you will have plenty of time to prepare your submissions in writing referred to in my ruling of a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me first check that you can hear the translation of my words in your own language. Please say yes if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber bids you good morning. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, and you will be subject to the procedure of the testimony of a witness, and I will explain the procedure in a moment. I first need to ask you your first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Andre Kujawinski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th September, 1965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were you born? In which town and which country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Liverpool, England.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession and position, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a warrant officer, Class 1, in the British Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, that is, more than ten years ago, what was your position in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a platoon sergeant in the British Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before an international or a national court regarding the facts related to 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have testified before this International Tribunal within another case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the name of the case in which you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've done two. Blaskic and -- I can't remember the name of the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you. I am going to ask you to please read the solemn declaration that Madam Usher is going to hand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have already testified, you are perfectly aware of the procedure applied in this International Tribunal. You will be answering questions that will be put to you by representatives of the Prosecution, who are seated to your right. After that stage of the proceedings, that is, the examination-in-chief, you will be asked questions by the Defence counsel, as the cross-examination, and the Defence counsel are seated on your left. There are six of them at present, but only two will have questions for you. The three Judges, who are in front of you, may if they feel it necessary to ask you questions, whenever they feel it necessary, either directly related to questions put to you by the Prosecution or by the Defence during the cross-examination or because simply the Judges feel that it is in the interest of justice to ask you to clarify certain points that you may not have mentioned or that require further clarification. If the questions are put to you clearly, try to answer them as fully and precisely as possible. If you don't understand the meaning of a question, please ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. If you don't know the answer, say so; if you do, please answer the question to the best of your knowledge. I need also to draw your attention to two other points. The first is that since you have taken the solemn declaration, this implies that you are bound to tell the whole truth. Should a witness be prompted to lie, he could be prosecuted for false testimony. A second point that shouldn't apply to you is that should in the course of the examination or cross-examination the witness be led to provide information that could be used against him, in that event the witness may refuse to answer, but the Chamber may compel him to answer, and if it does so, the Chamber guarantees a kind of immunity, which means that the evidence given cannot be used against the witness. Those would be in broad lines the procedure. However, as you have already appeared as a witness, you are accustomed to this procedure. Without wasting any time, and as it is Friday and we wouldn't wish you to spend another weekend in The Hague, I turn to the Prosecution and give them the floor for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President and Your Honours. And good morning. May it please you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Warrant Officer Kujawinski. Can you tell us where and within which unit you were deployed between November 1992 and May 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I was deployed in Vitez with the 1st Battalion, the 22nd Cheshire Regiment, and from there we worked out of Vitez into an area called Kladanj and up into Tuzla, and then for the final part I moved back to the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What -- briefly, in outline form, were the responsibilities of your unit?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: They changed whilst we were there. We'd been the first unit into the area. But in very short terms, we were escorting food convoys through the country to warehouses, where they were then distributed out to the areas within Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the 26th of April, 1993, in the morning of that day, did you set off for any particular assignment?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I was tasked by the ops room, which was in Vitez --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By the ...?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Ops room, operations room, which was in Vitez, to go with the UNHCR lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You need not call her name.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just tell us her -- what was her position?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: She was high ranking in the UNHCR, as far as I'm aware. And I went with her vehicle, her driver, and an interpreter, and two of my armoured vehicles to a village we called Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you -- what was the task? Why were you told that you needed to accompany her?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: There was reports given to her that atrocities had been done in the area. As to what, we were unaware. And we'd never been up this area before, so it was all new to the soldiers as such but not to the UNHCR. So we set off that day with the two armoured vehicles, with the Land Rover belonging to the -- to the UNHCR in the centre, which was a customary thing to do for protection at this time now because the area had developed into a worse state. I recall driving up the valley, passing through a roadblock, which was manned. By whom, I don't know. But we just drove straight through it. They just waved us through. And then we came to the village which was high up in the mountains. We could see roughly the -- the edge of the village, which was in a bend in the road and to the left was a river. We turned right, went up the mountain track, which was okay at this point, until we got to a very sharp left turn, where we then couldn't negotiate it with our armoured vehicles too -- too good. So as the commander, I decided then to leave one of the vehicles down at this point, also the border of the -- of the fighting was closing north anyway at this point. So I left that there for a tactical reason. And I then disembarked from the vehicle and continued to walk the ground in front of the vehicle to ensure in that it was steady on the ground. As I walked up, the ground was sloping away very sharply to the left and the vehicle was just about making it up in the track, in the sense of it falling off. We then came to what I believe was the village at the time of Miletici. It was a very small outcrop of houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many in the heart of the village, the centre of the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: In the centre of the village? Ten, ten houses. And then we came into what -- what I would call -- I still call it -- a square, which was just a clearing with the houses around it. We were closely followed obviously by the Land Rover of the UNHCR. We then tried immediately to turn the Warrior vehicle around, but it was quite impossible to do at this moment, so we just left everything, turned off, instead of making our presence too loud at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About what time you arrived there in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: It was late morning. It was late morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So what happened after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Everyone got off the vehicle, all nice and polite, as normal, to get a good hearts' and mind relationship going. And we leave one man on the vehicle and the remainder of us walk around, some five people. I then stuck very closely with the lady of the UNHCR, her Interpreter, and the driver of the Land Rover stayed with his vehicle. And we just continued -- or we just started walking round the village. I told the soldiers of mine, I just wanted them to be nosey as such, which means go for patrol around and let me know what you see. During this, the lady of the UNHCR started talking to several people in the village, which I noted at this point there was only old people there. There was no young people. They were all old. One of the soldiers then came back to me and informed me that he'd seen some dry blood on the floor, several pools of old dry blood, and said it was by a building over there, which we then called -- we then called from then on "the pink house," because it was painted pink. So discreetly I went over to the pink house, had a look towards the entrance, and at the entrance, which was at the rear of the square, and there was large pools of -- of blood there. So I came back to the lady of the UNHCR and through the interpreter - she was now talking to an old lady - and the conversation was going just about what -- what had happened. And the old lady was -- also, the group at this time were continuing to say that nothing had happened -- nothing had happened. After a long period of time - I couldn't recall how long - a very old lady then spoke out. She was very distraught. She was shaking. So we gave her a cup of tea because our vehicles can do all this facility. We then took her to the side, where she told us that people had been killed in the house, she told us. So at that point I tried to get a look in the window, which I did, after getting a lift up. I looked into the window, and I could see the walls were painted very light pink, compared to the outside, and inside there was blood strewn all over the walls. I -- what looked like it had been done with something sliding down the wall, whether it be clothing or whatever. From then on, my focus turned on to this house. No one else could see in the house at this point. So I asked the UNHCR lady -- or sorry, I informed the UNHCR lady what I'd saw, and we carried on with this lady all the time. It was now getting on very late in the day, and we hampered the lady to -- could we get into the house to find out more of what had happened. But she still wouldn't let us go anywhere near the house or wouldn't tell us anything. Eventually, a large period of time later, we were allowed into the house, but she only let myself and the UNHCR lady in. She just wouldn't let anyone else in. So we went into this house. I recall the door opening, after passing the blood. To the left was a cloakroom, clothes, shoes, coats hanging up and thrown on the floor. We then entered the main room of the house, which was the room I could see from the window. The window was now on the right. And on the left, there was a -- a wall, and on that wall there was a -- a crucifix and a picture of the Last Supper. At this point then I noticed a couch, which was below the window that I'd looked through, and this couch had large amounts of dark red blood, clots of blood and hair and pieces of bone scattered on the floor and on the couch, and cushions, and the cushions, after looking at them, had holes in them, and the holes had released feathers, which were on the settee also. I presumed at this point that they'd been used to -- to muffle explosion -- or gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mean the sounds of gunshots?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, the sounds, the sounds of gunshots. I continued to look around the house. The -- that room had another door, which was in the top left corner. I looked in there. There was nothing in there. I came back out. We comforted the old lady again, and -- and then we came out of the house. The door got locked behind us, and we thanked the woman and then we tried to get on to the lady to ask her where the bodies were, how many there was. But she wouldn't let any of that go. This day was now coming to a close. And a gentleman, young, not seen before, came to us unarmed and told us that we should leave the area very quickly. There was a large amount of soldiers making their way north to the border, BiH soldiers, he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To the border? What do you mean by "border"?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: The border where the fighting was taking place at this moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. So it was my decision, then, rapidly to leave the area. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you left, did the villagers or the old lady give you any inkling as to what had transpired in the pink house?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: She -- she told us that -- she had now informed us that young men had died. And what -- the way it came about, we asked her about the house and she said that that day -- that day soldiers had came into the village. And when she said the next word, we then all sort of, like, looked surprised. She said Mujahedin had come into the village. And they'd taken all the villagers and put them into a ruin. The ruin was just off the square and opposite the pink house. When they got them there, they segregated them and basically made two groups: A group of people who could fight and a people -- and a group of people that couldn't fight. And they let them go, that couldn't fight. According to the lady then, they got taken into the house, after being told to take up arms, which they refused. They got taken into the house and were tortured and executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did she say how many?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, she did not, not at this point. Not at this point. We were then still asking her how many, which is when this gentleman arrived, and it was my decision then to move out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: At this point, then, we made our way quicker down the track, met up with the other armoured vehicle, and went back to the main road junction, which had turned right to go up to the village by the river. And just as we got there, lots of trucks passed, crowded, packed. There were trucks. There was buses. There was every form of transport there. And it was making their way north full of BiH soldiers with the flags, waving the flags, waving all their -- all their guns, and cheering, joyful, because they were going into battle. So we just waved at them, and we turned off to the left and made our way back to Vitez, and it was now dark. We got to Vitez. I reported all what had happened to the ops room. Because prior to leaving -- sorry, I forgot to mention -- I put it to the interpreter that we could bring coffins to bury these people in the morning. And she agreed to that. So back to your last question: I did say to her, "How many coffins should we bring?" And she said, "Five."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And who were you speaking to when you asked that question?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: The UNHCR lady. I was speaking to her and she was speaking through the interpreter to the old lady again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we move on, I think you said that the old lady told you through the interpreters that the soldiers, the Mujahedin, had come that day. Is that what she said? Did she say they came that day or did she say they came before that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: They came before that day. Sorry. They -- yes, they came before that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So that night you reported what had transpired to your operations room. And were you subsequently tasked?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. They -- they decided that I should go back the next day with the same composite of vehicles, some extra men, and a -- a wheeled vehicle with the coffins in them, inside, which we picked up before departing to Miletici. We picked them up from a large warehouse in -- in Vitez. I decided at that point actually to pick up crosses as well, which were also in the same warehouse, due to the house having a crucifix and a picture of the Last Supper there, so I picked up crosses at that point, and then returned to the house -- or to the village the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What happened when you returned to the village that morning?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: We'd done the same set-up, where we left the vehicle at the bottom. But this time the extra wheeled vehicle came up to this now very small square. And once we got there, we found the old lady again, spoke to her in more detail, made her comfortable first, and then we started to ask her about the -- where the bodies were. And initially, again, she wouldn't tell us. She wouldn't let us go into the pink house again. That -- that had now passed. So we asked her where the bodies were. And again, after a period of time, she pointed to a house which was now on the far side of the square and -- with, like, a large veranda in front of it. Myself, one of my soldiers, and a gentleman who I'd brought with me, whose job now had changed and he was -- initially he was in charge of all the food distribution. He now also got put in charge of -- for want of a better word, body counting, if that's the right phrase to use. And he kept records of that. And him and the soldier and myself, with the old lady and the UNHCR lady and the interpreter, opened the door of the house and went into the house, where we believe these five bodies were laid. Upon opening the door, the smell was horrendous, and the bodies were laid out nice and -- nice and uniformly, in a straight line, all five of them. And we removed the five coffins one at a time, placed them on the veranda, and we placed a body into each coffin one at a time before loading it onto the vehicle. I only got to see closely three of the bodies. The first one I saw was -- had its knuckles, fingers, elbows, and even to one point a knee had been severely damaged, to the point that the finger had even been bent backwards. It was just unnatural, if that's the right word. It was unnatural. It was bent the wrong way. The other two bodies, one of them which was very bloated by this time, had had its -- or had had their throats cut with a -- a blunt instrument all the way around, completely around the throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say cut -- cut with a blunt instrument.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? Just tell us exactly what you saw.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: A large mark -- not mark. A large indentation around the whole of the neck. The head -- the head was still on the body. This instrument just didn't get through the neck bone, that's all. But then it was cut completely around. That was -- that was the second and third body. As they were getting onto -- or as the third one was being put onto the vehicle, I went outside the building and got hold of the interpreter to ask her to get around the village with this old lady to find out the names of these people. And she then came back to me with one piece of paper with all the names on it. I then -- I then wrote their names on individual pieces of paper and then asked the interpreter to check them off with the locals to make sure I'd spelt them right and not done anything wrong with them. At this point, then, it was all done, and we placed each piece of paper of the right person into the coffin before placing the lid on top, which was just -- it wasn't screwed down or nailed down anyway. We had the four -- the five crosses at this point. And before we got -- or as we got to the location where they were going to be buried, which we didn't know yet, I was going to write the names on with a permanent pen onto the crosses. So all the bodies now were on the vehicle, in the coffins, and we asked -- we asked the villagers - who in particular, I can't remember - we asked them, "Where should we take them?" And they told us to take them down the road to -- to a large church. There was a very -- it's a beautiful church, actually. And we made our way down the village -- down the road the way we'd come, off to this village. And as we got to the village, we were met by two monks who came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: It begins with "B." It's on the left-hand side as you drive down. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's okay. It's not an issue. Okay. So what did you do with the bodies?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: The monks met us. They told us could we reverse the truck back, and we'd done so. And then one by one -- no, sorry, two at a time we took the coffins to the side of the church, where lo and behold there was already graves dug for them. So someone had told someone that these bodies were coming. I also noted at this point that the village had lots of flags flying from lampposts, telegraph poles, rather, and trees, et cetera, and these were Croat flags, one of which I took off a tree. We then placed the coffins into the graves, and the -- one of the soldiers labeled all the crosses up with the names, put the lids back on, and then we said thank you to the monks and then we left at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. The bodies, were they all male or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, they were all male. And the ones that I saw -- the three that I saw were young, in the sense of not over 30, not -- not over 30 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you went there the first day, how long did you spend in Miletici that day, that is, the 26th? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Eight hours-ish. Approximately eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what was the condition of the buildings and the structure there is -- structures there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: It was a very left-alone village, so words to say. Out of the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Don't tell us a conclusion. Tell us what you saw about the -- the buildings.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: All right. I saw a very peaceful village, a very village -- a village that was out of the way, left alone. Again, as I say, approximately 10, 20 houses. They were just very happy getting on with themselves and that were ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you notice in way of damage to the structures there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, there was no -- there was no -- at this moment in time at the area we were working, no, this was a village that was different, to say the least; because there was no burnt-out houses. The only damaged house was one they called the ruin, but that was a ruin through age. There was no roof on it. The walls were falling down. But it wasn't damaged purposely. That was just age that had damaged it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the old lady told you about the Mujahedin. Did you know who she was speaking of? Had you been briefed about them or had you become aware of who she was referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: We, all of us, knew who she was speaking about because we had daily briefs on what was happening. Bosnia at this moment -- at that particular time had had mercenaries working in there, et cetera, and we all -- we got told about Mujahedin, and they were in the area, but no one had seen any. No one had heard of anything at this moment -- or at that moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "no one," you mean you had not seen or --

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- seen them.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Well, our soldiers had not seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: We had not seen any.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And your tour of duty in Bosnia ended when?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: It ended in the May of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stamp. I'll now turn to the Defence team for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kujawinski. Let me introduce myself. My name is Stephane Bourgon, and together with my colleagues, Mrs. Residovic and Mrs. Muriel Cauvin, we represent General Hadzihasanovic. I have a few questions for you based on both the context and exactly what you saw when you travelled to Miletici. Can I confirm, Mr. Kujawinski, that you were a platoon sergeant with BritBat and that you were a member of the Cheshire Regiment at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that you were deployed in Bosnia from November of 1992 until May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that your headquarters or where you were located was in Vitez and that was the area where both "A" Company and "C" Company were located?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the 26th of April, when you received that tasking to travel to Miletici, this came from the ops room, the operations room of your battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you yourself, Mr. Kujawinski, had never travelled to Miletici before.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, however, you had been at that moment for five months on the ground, and you were familiar with the roads and how to get to Miletici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Our vehicles were equipped with a satellite navigation equipment, and we also have maps, so -- to find your way around. You find your way anyway, yeah, there's no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And by that time, you had done a considerable amount of travelling in the area.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm that Miletici is approximately 20 kilometres north of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that Miletici is a very small and remote village way up in the hills?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Kujawinski, the hill to Miletici, as you described it, is a very steep, and the very is kind of a dead-end. There's no road further after the village.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct. From -- from the square. From the square there's no more roads out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the path leading to Miletici is very narrow, and as you described it, it was difficult for your vehicles to make it up the road.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you travelled to Miletici at that time, initially there were two Warriors and one Land Rover, and for protection purposes and because of the nature of the track you decided to leave one Warrior at the bottom of the hill.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Not at the very bottom. Midway. It was midway, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the distance between the bottom of the hill and where the village of Miletici is located is approximately 1 kilometre?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you arrived in the village, you described that you arrived to a small square. Would you agree with me that it was very difficult if only to turn around your vehicles to that you could face back down ready to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that time, you did not notice any battle damage or houses destroyed in any way, other from that house that was in ruins.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you arrived in the village, you said it was mid-morning.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also mentioned in one of your previous statements that you could not tell from what you saw arriving in Miletici whether the village was under the control of any one of the armies.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Miletici, based on your military knowledge, is not a place where you would expect a military attack to take place.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And upon your arrival in Miletici, as you mentioned, there were no young people, no young men, and all you could see was very old people.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the people you met at that time told you that you were the first ones or the first international patrol to make it there for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct. And I could tell that from the use of the track as well I was coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned to my colleague that you remained until it was getting dark. What time would that have been?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: An estimate, 7.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kujawinski. Now, the woman you spoke to, there was one old -- very old woman you spoke to, and you mentioned she was very distressed by the whole situation. She mentioned to you that the Mujahedin had come into the village and had gathered everyone into the centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Into the ruin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And again, I'm just taking some statements or some lines from your statement that you provided the Office of the Prosecution. The Mujahedin segregated the group, and they let go the woman and the males who were too old to fight.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the Mujahedin at that time were not from the local area, from what they could tell you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the men who remained in the village were then asked to take up arms and fight for the Mujahedin, but these men refused; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And upon refusing to fight for the Mujahedin, then they were taken into this house, where they were somehow killed.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Eventually you yourself, Mr. Kujawinski, made it into the pink house. And one of the things you saw was the cushions or the pillows, which you assumed had been used to muffle gunshots.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm curious. When you mentioned "to muffle gunshots," is that based on your military knowledge? And my question is as follows: Based on what you know of using a cushion to muffle a gunshot, would a person standing around 100 to 200 metres from that house, could they hear the shots being fired through that cushion?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I don't know the answer. I've -- I've never shot a -- a rifle through a cushion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So that assumption that you made at that point was based on what?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: On -- on what I'd saw with my eyes but from seeing things on TV probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And by that time you were not aware of how many bodies had been killed.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the lady you were with and yourself, you succeeded in convincing the old lady or -- sorry, maybe -- I'll take that again. You did not convince the old lady to show you the bodies, but you convinced her to visit the pink house.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it is where you saw that scene in the pink house.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, it is at that moment that the man approached you to inform you about the huge number of soldiers travelling on the road which you had taken to go up to that house.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Once we came out of the house, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you actually met these soldiers after you had made your way back down and had reunited with the vehicle that was left midway up the hill.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this man did not tell you which soldiers they were or which units they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: He did mention, however, that they were going to fight towards the Serb front line.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you met these people, they were basically friendly. They seemed to be in high spirits. And there was actually no reason for you to be rushing anywhere because of these soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the next day, you returned to -- to Miletici, and at that time you were accompanied by Sergeant Major Arthur; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The sergeant major was not there the day before.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was the lady from UNHCR present that second day?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: She was there. And so you saw the bodies. You placed them in coffins. You took pictures. And then you took them down to a church.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, to -- in answer to a question from my colleague, he asked you the name of the town where you took the bodies.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier on that you did not remember. From the material I have on your previous testimony, once you said it was Guca Gora, once you said it was Brajkovici. Would that help you in determining where, to what village you took these bodies?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Guca Gora. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the villagers that morning, they saw that you were UNPROFOR, that you were there to help, and they started to speak a little more.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And again, they told you that the Mujahedin had killed the five men and that they had never seen these individuals before.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where you took the bodies - now you mentioned Guca Gora - you determined that this was a Croat village because there were Croatian flags all over the place and on the lampposts around Guca Gora; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I wouldn't determine it was a Croat place, because at that moment in time in Bosnia flags were everywhere and it didn't necessarily mean that that area was Croat. It -- it meant that Croats had either passed through the area, had left their sign everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you yourself, Mr. Kujawinski, at that time had not determined whether the five bodies you were carrying, to what religion they were from.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you got back to your battalion on both days, the initial day and the second day, all of this information was reported to the ops room.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you explain how this information is reported to the ops room.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Okay. Before you go out on a -- on a mission or on an operation, you're briefed up. You're told what your task is to do. You then ask your questions. You then book out, which means log report going out and where you're going to. You then keep in communications via the radio whilst you're out. You do the task at hand. And then when you return back to the camp, you report back into the ops room straight away as a commander. And then you are -- or you debrief the people on what you've seen. You go to the int cell, you tell them if things have changed, et cetera. And therefore, everything is kept up to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And such a debriefing would be done orally with the ops room or the intelligence cell.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, and logged down in some cases. For example, if you were talking over the radio whilst you were out, it would be logged, it would be written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kujawinski, the -- my colleague asked you a question concerning the knowledge you had about the Mujahedin at that time.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I recall when you testified in the Blaskic case you basically gave the same answer as you did today. You said that the information you had at the time was that there were mercenaries, they operated in small pockets, they were ruthless people who would stop at nothing to get what they want. And that's basically the knowledge you had of what was a Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A few more questions. The bodies when you saw them that morning, the second day, was your conclusion that these bodies had been there for quite some time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Upon walking into the house, there was a -- a rancid smell. And the -- one of -- I think it was the third body of the five was very bloated. It was -- his legs, his arms, his stomach, everything was bloated about him, which told me --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: These events were not recent, at least to you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, they weren't recent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you testified in the Kupreskic case, a question was put to you concerning your knowledge that people had been expelled from the village or driven out of the village. And your answer at that time was that you had no knowledge of this. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying also that you had no knowledge that some of those people wanted to move to Nova Bila and that in fact there was some people moved to Nova Bila at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on both of these occasions when you were in Miletici, the first day and the second day, no one else from the British Battalion travelled up there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not see anyone from ECMM or the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not see anyone up there from the joint command.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kujawinski. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, this concludes the cross-examination on behalf of the accused General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now addressing the other Defence team. Do you have any questions for this witness, Mr. Dixon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We don't have any questions on behalf of Mr. Kubura for this witness. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber has a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you arrived the first time and you met the old lady and you were about to discover that something happened, you said that you were on the radio. Did you warn your superiors by radio that there had been a problem in that village?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No. No, we had no -- we had no radio communication between ourselves and our ops room at this point. We were speaking directly to the vehicle below, who were then relaying the message back to our ops room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you arrived with the person who represented the UNHCR and who, according to what you said, had certain information, when one travels with someone or accompanies someone it is normal to exchange a few words. Did she tell you where the information had come from? Because you were on that mission because UNHCR knew that something had happened there.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't told what I might encounter within the village. All I was told was that I was going to this village because there had been reports of atrocities in the area, not in that particular village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the lady from the UNHCR who was with you, she didn't tell you anything more? She didn't know anything, in fact? Or maybe she did know but she didn't tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Maybe -- maybe so. She didn't -- she did not tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: You said that a young man told you that you should leave because forces were arriving and that they were numerous. Why did you leave? What were you afraid of? Why did you leave? What were the risks? If you were there, since -- if the regular army was arriving, why go away?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Many risks. The first one was that it was a -- it was a practice that we never stayed out overnight. For what reasons, operational, I don't know, but we never stayed out overnight. Secondly, that the -- the young -- or the man told us that lots of soldiers were coming. He didn't say how many. But when we got to the bottom of the hill, I'm glad we did leave. But upon seeing them and the mood they were in, the joyful mood they were in, they -- they weren't a threat at that time. But we left purely because night-time was falling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So those who were arriving, according to what you are saying, you did see them coming.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: We saw them coming as we got to the bottom of the hill. They were just passing us on the bend where we had turned right to go up to Miletici. And as I explained, they were in several -- lots of vehicles of different kinds, packed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the soldiers that you saw, were they in camouflage uniform or in civilian clothing? How would you describe the men you saw at the bottom of the hill?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: The majority were in uniform, but then amongst them there was a lot of mixed -- mixed uniform, which is maybe a military top with a civilian pair of trousers or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there must have been officers or commanders with them. Why didn't you inform the commander of those arriving soldiers what you had established, that there had been a serious incident in a certain house and that you had seen traces of blood? Why didn't you inform members of the army of what you had seen on the spot, since you were not at war against the people you saw?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Communication between us, the -- the British soldiers, and the two factions at this time wasn't there. We -- we as the soldiers on the ground had very, very, if any, communication with the soldiers. So to me it wasn't worth telling them what had gone on anyway. No. I wouldn't have spoken to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Defence have any additional questions following the answers given by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just two very short questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... To the questions put to you by the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber. Can you confirm that the soldiers you met at the bottom of the hill were not travelling to Miletici whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No. No, the soldiers we met at the bottom of the hill were going north. Just as we got to the bottom of the hill, one or two vehicles had just passed us and they stopped, or they slowed down, and they -- they were carrying on north through the valley, going to their front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To try and picture the scene, would I be right in saying that there's a road leading north to the front line and you were coming kind of a T-junction going towards Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yeah, a Y-junction, to my -- to my recollection. They were coming up the valley, a steep -- obviously, a valley, steep sides. The river is on the left. And we were coming down to meet this road and we had to do a very sharp left turn to go back down the valley the opposite way to what they were travelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you knew, Mr. Kujawinski, that the front line with the Serbs was further north, about 7 to 8 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yeah. I think it was 10 kilometres at the time, which rings a bell. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it wasn't unusual for you to see troops going towards the front line because troops at the front line were changing regularly.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: This amount of troops that I saw that day was the biggest, was the largest amount of troops I'd seen in Bosnia in one collective group. I saw another large group which was several days, in fact, or -- if not a week later in the Zenica area. But this was the largest amount of troops in one collective group I'd seen to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nothing, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have some more questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Mr. Kujawinski, on your second visit to Miletici, on the 27th, if I understood you well, you came back with the lady from the UNHCR and you entered the house and you saw a number of bodies. The way you described it implicated, I would say, that you had the impression that some crimes had been committed, that these people were murdered. Is that your impression?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, my belief is they were -- they were executed, killed, some of them, after being tortured in the pink house, which also the old lady told us would now become a shrine, the pink house. And they had then been moved to the building opposite the square, where we then saw them for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So the place where you saw they were murdered was a different place from the place where you then found the bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: At that point did you or any other person from your company or maybe the lady from the UNHCR make notes or make -- make drawings or make pictures from the situation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I -- everywhere I went for the six-month tour of Bosnia, I carried a camera, a small -- at the time. I think they're now extinct. A C110 film camera, and I took photographs everywhere. I also kept a diary for the six months, all of which I've handed over -- over to the court. And over reading my statements over the past few days, I've actually -- as I was reading my statement, before I got to the part of mentioning all this, I -- in fact, I've got it in front of me here now, I think. I drew the courtyard itself and where the houses were, et cetera. That is still very much so alive in my -- in my head still. But at the moment in time there, no, I didn't draw anything. I don't recall -- I don't recall the lady doing anything like that neither.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I understand you. Did you take drawings or photographs at that moment?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: At that moment, I took photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. And you said you handed them over to the court.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: This Tribunal, you mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: To the investigators?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And when was that, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: I can't recall. I can't recall exactly when it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Was it years after the event or ...?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Oh, yeah -- well, yes, two years after. Three years after. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Two years after the event. When you came back to your base in Vitez, I understand, you did report your findings to the intelligence officer or to -- to another person. Do you know whether BritBat itself, you yourself, or any other person informed also the local authorities there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: That, I cannot answer. I mean, our -- my chain of command is -- is to -- once you get into the -- into the camp, is for the commander, which was myself, to disembark the vehicle, tell everybody what to do. For example, the driver. You check the vehicle. You check the ammunition. So on and so forth. Whilst they do so, "Don't move. I'll be back in a minute." I then go to the ops room. First thing I do is book back in or report back in, my call sign. I'm now back in. I then tell them briefly what has happened, in the sense of where I've been, what I've done, et cetera, although they should have kept all that from the radio log. I then go next door, which is the intelligence room, and sit down and be debriefed by the intelligence cell about what I saw and then they update things from the -- and everything, to my knowledge, is then logged, recorded. Whether they tell other authorities, I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. So, you're not aware of steps being taken by BritBat on the basis of your report in the way of informing other authorities or international organisations or whatever?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an additional question for you. But in view of the nature of the question, I should like to ask, Mr. Registrar, that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a couple questions in respect to the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you handed over the photographs you'd taken to officers of this Tribunal a couple years after the incidents that you just described. You -- is it correct that you handed them over in respect to a different investigation of another case and not this case?

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Correct. When I -- on the first interview that I was -- or that -- on the first interview that I'd undertaken, I was asked to produce anything that I had, and I produced this photo album.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDRE KUJAWINSKI
utterances.text: Which is the six months in a book. I can tell you now. And I handed that over. The diary I was never returned for approximately four years, but I did get the original back. And the photographs, they took them out the book, copied them, and returned everything back to its normal way, and that's the way I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn for the last time to Defence counsel to ask them whether they have any questions. If not, Witness -- some more questions, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not a question. But I think that you are about to release the witness, Mr. President. Before he's released, may I just indicate that of the photographs he took three are copies of three that were relevant to Miletici remain here. The rest were given back to him. Instructions had been given that he be asked to carry what he had for this case, but there was some misunderstanding because the Victims and Witnesses Unit, not knowing about photographs or anything like that, in their instructions to him told him that he needed not bring anything, that he would be taken care of when he arrived. So when he was came and he was asked about these photographs he told us that he was told not to bring anything. But the Victims and Witnesses Unit told him not to bring anything for a different purpose. So -- but there are three photographs here. They are not on the exhibit list, so they were not produced. However, Mr. President, Your Honours, having indicated some interest in the photographs, perhaps if -- if efforts were made, they could be brought before the Court before he's released. It's really a possibility I leave open to the Court. That is all I have to say on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that the Prosecution would like to tender these three photographs and to tender them they have to be identified by the witness, and also you have to have them in your hands. So the first questions: Do you have those photographs or do you not have them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I do not have them in my hands. They are in the building. They can be found. We had no intentions, we did not propose to tender them. I just am making the information available to the Court, since the Court did express some interest in the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this matter, we will deliberate subsequently. We consider the examination to be over. We thank you for coming. We wish you a safe journey home. And I'm going to ask Madam Usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we have a few minutes left before the break, and perhaps even the adjournment, could the Prosecution tell us what the schedule is for next week, in view of the latest information that they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, for this purpose could we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. I'll start again. We would like to thank the Trial Chamber for allowing us to rapidly analyse the decision rendered earlier this morning, the decision that has to do with the admissibility of documents. During the break, we analysed the consequences of this decision for the Defence. And at this point in time, Mr. President, we would like to make some comments. We don't want to go back on the decision, but we would like to comment on this. Our comments will consist of two parts: There are over 650 documents, Mr. President, that have to do with admission into evidence and have to do with the relevance and the authenticity of the documents. These things have to be justified for each document. We will need, I think, about half a page. We believe that the request the Trial Chamber has made for our response is a document that would have between 200 and 300 pages. We don't think that we can draft such a document by the deadline indicated by the Trial Chamber; namely, the 8th of April. We believe that we will need about six weeks in order to produce such a document. Six weeks at least. As far as the comments that the Defence would like to make, we've had the opportunity of examining the decision, but we would need a little more time to analyse the legal consequences and the legal position of the accused in relation to such a debate. We believe that there might be consequences for the accused. It has to do with the burden of proof that is to be borne by the Prosecution. And with regard to the position of the accused in all criminal proceedings. For these reasons, Mr. President, we would like to have a few days to carefully analyse the decision and to carefully analyse the legal consequences. At the moment, we haven't made any decisions, but we might make some subsequent comments to the Trial Chamber, which might take the form of a request for a clarification of this decision or re-examination of this decision. As I have said, we believe that the consequences might be quite important for both accused in this case. With regard to the documents, this is a matter that the Chamber has been interested in from the very beginning of the trial. We think it might be useful to make some written comments and submit these comments to you, Mr. President, in order to take a decision about this subject, given the consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon and then Mr. Withopf. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The only additional point I wish to make in supporting Mr. Bourgon's submissions, Your Honours, is the point that was highlighted when we first addressed Your Honours on this matter, and that is the one -- of the difficulty we face in being able to when we have so many documents understand what reliance the Prosecution is placing on these documents in order for us to respond in accordance with Your Honours' order. We have the pre-trial brief, which mentions some of these documents, but only a handful of -- of the over 600 documents. And we would -- and this may be a matter that we put forward to Your Honours in further submissions. But we would request that some consideration be given to the Prosecution outlining the way in which they wish to use these documents, what reliance they wish to place upon them, so that we can respond to them accordingly. It's of course not unreasonable to ask the Defence to respond to what the Prosecution's case is. But if we do not know what it is at this point in relation to those documents, us in responding, it might mean we are not responding to the correct issues. But in addition to that, we might be putting forward our defence way before our Defence case is in fact due to be presented, which is after the Prosecution case. And that is a matter which we are concerned about. If the order that Your Honours have made could take that point into account and request the Prosecution as part of their case to indicate what the use will -- or what use will be made of these document, we would be most grateful. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the issue of tendering the documents and all related issues have been discussed since months and they have been discussed in each and every detail possible during court sessions, outside court sessions, in informal meetings. The Chamber has now after having had all information before it, has now rendered an informed decision. Defence is now telling us that they wish - and there are very clear indications - that they wish to file a motion for reconsideration. If they file a motion for reconsideration, the Prosecution would have the right to respond to this motion. That would mean another two, three weeks will pass by without any further decision on this issue. The Prosecution anticipates that the Prosecution's case will be finished by early June 2004 at the very latest. If Defence is telling us now that they are not in a position to elaborate on the reasons why they challenge the Prosecution's documents not prior to six weeks from now on and the Prosecution would have the right to respond obviously, and the Chamber would then have to make a decision, that would be, what is quite obvious, after the closing of the Prosecution's case. It appears to be a bit odd to proceed in such a manner. One would have thought, Mr. President, Your Honours - and I'm making reference to paragraph 3 of the recent submission, of the recent filing of Defence on this issue in which they have communicated what they think the challenges may be, and they identified at least ten different issues. One would have thought that at this point in time Defence would know which challenges they wish to make in respect to each and every document. The documents are in -- are in possession of the Defence since many months. Quite a number of them, actually, since more than two years. It appears to be a bit difficult to now at the eleventh hour think about what the challenges could be. Therefore, the Prosecution opposes any already-announced motion for reconsideration of this decision. However, if the Chamber allows the Defence to file such a motion, the Prosecution would of course exercise its right to respond to such a motion. Finally, the practice which has now been applied by the decision of the Trial Chamber on this very same issue is very much in consistence with the practice applied by a number of Trial Chambers or by other Trial Chambers in a number of proceedings before this Tribunal. Therefore, the Prosecution respectfully requests the Trial Chamber to not allow the Defence to again and again discuss this issue. We reached a point in time in the course of the proceedings this matter must be finally decided, and the Trial Chamber has decided on this issue in order to allow this trial go in the same speed it has went over the past. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence has told us that they will reflect on the matter to see whether the decision might not have legal consequences for the Defence that concern the burden of proof, which is placed naturally on the Prosecution. It is not for the Defence to bear the burden of proof. The Defence reminded us of this legal principle, and quite rightly. But that is not the issue. The decision that was rendered, as we have emphasised, states that 650 documents can't be tendered into evidence while the witnesses appear here. So we want to make a distinction. We want to see which documents out of the 650 documents have been contested by the Defence. But the Trial Chamber would like to have more information about why they're contested, information about the authenticity or the relevance of the documents. This would enable everyone to see the matters more clearly. So the Defence has told us that at the moment they think that each document should require half a page. That would be 300 pages if we're dealing with 650 documents. So perhaps half a page is required for some documents but there might be other documents that only require one line. The best thing to do would be for the Defence to continue to reflect about this issue over the weekend, because you have two days before you now, and on Monday, when we start with the hearing, you can inform us of your position. And we will see whether we will give you leave to file a motion requesting that we clarify our decision, because in our opinion the decision was very clear. So you have two days to think about the matter. It would be best to take stock of the matter at the beginning of the hearing next Monday. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence is aware of the fact that the Trial Chamber rendered its decision, and we would like -- we don't want to have the document revised. Or if it is, it should only be done in accordance with the regulations. So our position is to confirm in all respects the decision of the Trial Chamber. But we would like to inform the Trial Chamber that the work involved is considerable. This would require more than two weeks of work to make our first assessment without drafting anything. So we would like to inform the Trial Chamber that this involves a lot of work and it can't be completed by the 8th of April. We wanted six weeks' time to be granted. And as far as the decision itself is concerned, Mr. President, as the Trial Chamber has asked us to do, we will think about this matter over the weekend in order to assess what the legal consequences of the decision might be, and we will inform the Trial Chamber of our position on Monday. We'll inform you whether we would like the decision to be reconsidered or whether other avenues should be explored. But, Mr. President, it's important to say that this issue, in spite of the comments made by my colleague from the Prosecution, from the very beginning of the first -- of the trial we started discussing the admissibility of documents and the difference between the admissibility of a document and the probative value of a document. The Prosecution's position with regard to documents which are as ordinary as maps that show the sites of crimes referred to in the indictment, the Prosecution in respect of such documents also raised objections. So this has a lot of consequences and gives rise to a lot of debate. We believe that the decision rendered by the Trial Chamber is one that requires a lot of time for us to consider its consequences.
